Project Python Foundations: FoodHub Data Analysis¶

Context¶

The number of restaurants in New York is increasing day by day. Lots of students and busy professionals rely on those restaurants due to their hectic lifestyles. Online food delivery service is a great option for them. It provides them with good food from their favorite restaurants. A food aggregator company FoodHub offers access to multiple restaurants through a single smartphone app.

The app allows the restaurants to receive a direct online order from a customer. The app assigns a delivery person from the company to pick up the order after it is confirmed by the restaurant. The delivery person then uses the map to reach the restaurant and waits for the food package. Once the food package is handed over to the delivery person, he/she confirms the pick-up in the app and travels to the customer's location to deliver the food. The delivery person confirms the drop-off in the app after delivering the food package to the customer. The customer can rate the order in the app. The food aggregator earns money by collecting a fixed margin of the delivery order from the restaurants.

Objective¶

The food aggregator company has stored the data of the different orders made by the registered customers in their online portal. They want to analyze the data to get a fair idea about the demand of different restaurants which will help them in enhancing their customer experience. Suppose you are hired as a Data Scientist in this company and the Data Science team has shared some of the key questions that need to be answered. Perform the data analysis to find answers to these questions that will help the company to improve the business.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different data related to a food order. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

Data Dictionary¶

  • order_id: Unique ID of the order
  • customer_id: ID of the customer who ordered the food
  • restaurant_name: Name of the restaurant
  • cuisine_type: Cuisine ordered by the customer
  • cost_of_the_order: Cost of the order
  • day_of_the_week: Indicates whether the order is placed on a weekday or weekend (The weekday is from Monday to Friday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday)
  • rating: Rating given by the customer out of 5
  • food_preparation_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the restaurant to prepare the food. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the restaurant's order confirmation and the delivery person's pick-up confirmation.
  • delivery_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the delivery person to deliver the food package. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the delivery person's pick-up confirmation and drop-off information

Question 3: Are there any missing values in the data? If yes, treat them using an appropriate method. [1 mark]¶

In [8]:
# Write your code here

# checking for any missing values in all the columns
data.isnull().sum()
# There are missing values in the dataset

# Hovever the 'rating' column is stored as an object type because it includes the string 'Not given'.
# Since ratings can only be between 1 to 5, 'Not given' should be treated as a missing value (NaN).
# However, around 40% of ratings are missing, which is quite significant.
# Imputing such a large portion of data may introduce bias, especially since ratings are subjective.
# Therefore, we will keep 'Not given' as NaN to accurately represent unrated orders.
# After replacement, the column will be converted to a numeric type.

data['rating'] = data['rating'].replace('Not given', np.nan)
# data['rating'] = data['rating'].replace(['Not given'], np.nan)

# we can confirm that we have replaces the value
data['rating'].unique()

# converting the rating field to float
data['rating'] = data['rating'].astype(float)

# Checking the propertion of missing values
data['rating'].value_counts(normalize=True, dropna=False)
Out[8]:
proportion
rating
NaN 0.387777
5.0 0.309800
4.0 0.203372
3.0 0.099052

Observations:¶

There are no explicit missing values in the dataset.

However, based on business understanding, not all customers provide ratings for their orders — these cases are recorded as 'Not given'. For accurate analysis and better visualization, the 'rating' field was converted to a numeric type (float), and 'Not given' values were replaced with NaN to properly represent missing ratings.

Observations:¶

The dataset contains 1898 records (orders) and 9 columns.

  • It covers information about orders, customers, restaurants, cuisines, ratings, and time taken for food preparation and delivery.

  • No explicit missing values are reported, but the 'rating' column includes 'Not given' now converted to Nan entries, representing missing feedback (~39% of total).

  • The order_id field contains 1,898 unique, sequential values ranging from 1476547 to 1478444 confirming that each record represents a distinct order with no duplicates.

  • The customer_id field contains 1898 values ranging from 1311 to 405334 indicating there are multiple unique customers, some of whom have placed the 1 or more orders during the time period represented in the dataset.

  • The dataset includes 178 restaurants, with “Shake Shack” being the most ordered from, accounting for ~11.5% (219/1898) of total orders.

  • There are a total of 14 unique cuisines, However American cuisine dominates the dataset, contributing roughly 30% of total orders.

  • The average order costs around $16.5, with most orders priced between $12 and $22. The cost distribution is slightly right-skewed, with a few higher-value orders.

  • There are 2 categories for the day_of_the_week, Weekday and Weekend, where most orders around 71% of the orders occur on weekends, suggesting higher food delivery activity during weekend.

  • There are 4 unique values for Rating 3,4,5 and Not Given / Nan. Ratings are mostly positive (4&5), However around 39% of the orders remains unrated. The overall feedback trends towards higher satisfaction or it can also indicate that most customers only leave a rating when the experience is positive.

  • Food preparation times are consistent across orders, averaging around 27 minutes, with standard deviation of around 4.63. The narrow range (20–35 mins) suggests standardized cooking processes among restaurants.

  • Deliveries take about 24 minutes on average ranging from 15 - 33 mins, and most are completed within 20–28 minutes (25% - 75%), with a standard deviation of 4.97 a little higher than food preparation time. The small variation indicates reliable delivery performance across restaurants.

  • Overall Observation

    • American Cusine and weekend orders are dominating the overall business.
    • Average order costs ~ $16.5, with food preparation and delivery time shows a consistent patterns of around 27 and 24 mins respectively.
    • Overall customer satisfaction is high, although a large portion of orders ~39% remains unrated.

Question 5: How many orders are not rated? [1 mark]¶

In [10]:
# Write the code here

# Checking the missing values and percentage of it.
data['rating'].value_counts(normalize=False, dropna=False)

# Count how many orders do not have a rating
unrated_orders = data['rating'].isna().sum()



# Total number of orders
total_orders = data.shape[0]

# Calculate percentage of unrated orders
unrated_percentage = (unrated_orders / total_orders) * 100


print(f"Number of unrated orders: {unrated_orders}")
print(f"Percentage of unrated orders: {unrated_percentage:.2f}%") # need to add :.2f to round the float to 2 digits

Number of unrated orders: 736
Percentage of unrated orders: 38.78%

Observations:¶

About 39% of the orders are not rated, indicating that a large portion of customers chose not to provide feedback.

Since this is a significant share of the data, imputing these missing ratings could create bias in the analysis.

Therefore, these missing ratings are retained as valid missing values (NaN) to accurately represent unrated orders.

Observations¶

  • The order_id field contains 1,898 unique, sequential values ranging from 1,476,547 to 1,478,444, confirming that each record represents a distinct order with no duplicates.

  • The customer_id field contains 1,898 values ranging from 1,311 to 405,334, indicating there are multiple unique customers.

    • Around 65% of customers placed only one order,
    • One customer placed 13 orders, the highest in the dataset.

  • The dataset includes 178 restaurants,

    • “Shake Shack” being the most ordered from, accounting for approximately 11.5% (219 out of 1,898) of total orders.
    • The top three restaurants (Shake Shack, The Meatball Shop, and Blue Ribbon Sushi) together account for around 25% of all orders.
    • The last 50 restaurants have only one order each, and the last 100 restaurants have at most four orders per restaurant.

  • There are a total of 14 unique cuisines.

    • However, American cuisine dominates the dataset, contributing roughly 30% of total orders.
    • The top three cuisines (American, Japanese, and Italian) combined account for around 71% of all orders,
    • Bottom six cuisines (Thai, French, Southern, Korean, Spanish, and Vietnamese) together represent only 4.5% of total orders.

  • The average order cost is around $16.5, with most orders priced between $12 and $22.

    • The cost distribution is right-skewed, with a few higher-value orders.

  • There are two categories for day_of_the_week: Weekday and Weekend.

    • About 71% of orders occur on weekends, suggesting higher food delivery activity during weekends.

  • There are four unique values for rating: 3, 4, 5, and Not Given/NaN.

    • Ratings are mostly positive (4 and 5); however, around 39% of orders remain unrated.
    • This trend suggests that customers tend to rate only when they are satisfied, indicating possible positive bias in the feedback.

  • Food preparation times are consistent across orders, averaging around 27 minutes, with a standard deviation of 4.63.

    • The narrow range (20–35 minutes) suggests standardized cooking processes among restaurants.

  • Delivery times average around 24 minutes, ranging from 15 to 33 minutes.

    • Most deliveries are completed within 20–28 minutes (25th–75th percentile), with a standard deviation of 4.97, slightly higher than food preparation time.
    • The small variation indicates reliable delivery performance across restaurants.

weekend_data = data[data['day_of_the_week'] == 'Weekend']

# Find the most popular cuisine on weekends
popular_weekend_cuisine = weekend_data['cuisine_type'].value_counts().idxmax()
popular_weekend_cuisine_count = weekend_data['cuisine_type'].value_counts().max()

print(f"Most popular cuisine on weekends: {popular_weekend_cuisine} ({popular_weekend_cuisine_count} orders)")

Most popular cuisine on weekends: American (415 orders)

Observations:¶

  • The most popular cuisine on weekends is American, consistent with its dominance in the overall dataset.
    • Weekend orders account for around 71% of total orders, and American cuisine remains the top choice, with 415 weekend orders — approximately 22% of all orders.
    • This shows that customer preference for American cuisine is consistently strong, even during weekends when order volume is highest.

Observations¶

  1. Cuisine Popularity vs Day of the Week All cuisines experience higher order volumes on weekends. Popular cuisines such as American, Japanese, and Italian dominate both weekdays and weekends, while niche cuisines like Thai and French see sharp weekend spikes — indicating customers tend to explore diverse or premium cuisines more during weekends.

  2. Food Preparation Time vs Day of the Week Most cuisines maintain stable preparation times across weekdays and weekends (~27 minutes average). However, a few cuisines (e.g., Thai, Mexican, Korean) show longer prep times on weekends (Thai: 24 → 29 min; Mexican: 24 → 28 min) likely due to increased order volume. Conversely, French and Chinese cuisines have slightly longer prep times on weekdays, suggesting variation based on kitchen workload or staffing.

  3. Cuisine vs Food Preparation Time Preparation times across cuisines are tightly grouped between 25 – 28 minutes, showing consistent operational efficiency. Cuisines like Chinese, Japanese, and Southern average around 27.5 minutes, while Vietnamese and Korean tend to prepare faster (~25 min), possibly because of simpler or pre-prepared dishes.

  4. Cuisine vs Delivery Time Delivery times are also consistent (mean ≈ 24 min) with minimal differences across cuisines. Korean and Vietnamese dishes show shorter delivery windows (~21–26 min), while French and Italian cuisines take slightly longer (~25–26 min). This suggests that cuisine type influences preparation more than delivery logistics.

  5. Cuisine vs Cost of Order French, Southern, Thai, and Spanish cuisines have higher average order costs (~19–20 dollars), indicating premium menu pricing. Moderate-priced cuisines (American, Italian, Chinese, Japanese) form the bulk of orders (≈16 dollars mean), while Korean and Vietnamese cuisines remain budget-friendly (under 15 dollars). The overall range (≈5 – 35 dollars) reflects a balanced mix of affordable and high-end offerings.

  6. Cuisine vs Average Rating Customer satisfaction remains high across cuisines (average rating > 4.2). Top-rated cuisines include Spanish (4.83) and Thai (4.67) — both smaller segments with strong positive feedback. Mainstream cuisines (American, Italian, Japanese, Chinese) also sustain solid ratings (~4.3–4.4), showing quality consistency despite large order volumes.

  7. Correlation Insights No strong correlations were found between cost, rating, and preparation/delivery time. This implies that customer satisfaction is not directly affected by how long food takes to prepare or deliver, but more likely by overall food quality and taste.

  8. Business Implication

Operational focus: Maintain the stable prep and delivery efficiency seen in major cuisines while monitoring weekend bottlenecks in Thai and Mexican restaurants.

Marketing: Highlight top-rated cuisines like Spanish and Thai during promotions.

Pricing: Premium cuisines already command higher prices — explore bundle offers or loyalty programs for moderately priced, high-volume cuisines to maximize revenue.

data_count_over_50['restaurant_name']

data_over_50_with_rating

Question 14: The company charges the restaurant 25% on the orders having cost greater than 20 dollars and 15% on the orders having cost greater than 5 dollars. Find the net revenue generated by the company across all orders. [3 marks]¶

In [34]:
# Write the code here
# find if the order has commision of 25%, 15% or none
def compute_comm(x):
    if x > 20:
        return x*0.25
    elif x > 5:
        return x*0.15
    else:
        return x*0

# add a new field commision for each order
data['commission'] = data['cost_of_the_order'].apply(compute_comm)

# Calculate total revenue generated by the company
total_revenue = data['commission'].sum()

print(f"Total revenue generated by the company: ${total_revenue:.2f}")

print("\n ")
def commission_type(x):
    if x > 20:
        return '25%'
    elif x > 5:
        return '15%'
    else:
        return '0%'

data['commission_type'] = data['cost_of_the_order'].apply(commission_type)

# Count how many orders fall in each category
commission_counts = data['commission_type'].value_counts().reset_index()
commission_counts.columns = ['Commission Type', 'Order Count']

print(commission_counts)

Observations:¶

  • The company generated a total commission revenue of 6,166.30 dollars from all 1,898 orders.
  • Around 70% (1,334) orders were charged at the 15% commission rate.
  • Around 29% (555) orders were charged at the 25% commission rate.
  • Around 0.5% (9) orders were incurred with no commission.

This indicates that while most orders are moderately priced and contribute steady earnings, nearly one-third of high-value orders (greater than 20 dollars) account for a significant portion of the total revenue, demonstrating the effectiveness of the tiered commission structure.

This suggests that order cost does not strongly influence delivery delays, as both low- and high-value orders experience similar wait times.

    data.groupby('day_of_the_week')['delivery_time']
    .agg([
        ('count', 'count'),
        ('mean', 'mean'),
        ('median', 'median'),
        ('Q1 (25%)', lambda x: x.quantile(0.25)),
        ('Q3 (75%)', lambda x: x.quantile(0.75))
    ])
    .round(2)
    .reset_index()
)

print(delivery_time_stats)

Observations:¶

The average delivery time on weekdays (28.3 minutes) is noticeably higher than on weekends (22.5 minutes), with similar trends seen in median and quartile values. This suggests that deliveries are generally faster on weekends, possibly due to less weekday traffic congestion or more flexible delivery scheduling on weekends.

Conclusion and Recommendations¶

Question 17: What are your conclusions from the analysis? What recommendations would you like to share to help improve the business? (You can use cuisine type and feedback ratings to drive your business recommendations.) [6 marks]¶

Conclusions:¶

  • Overall Operations Efficiency

    • The company maintains a highly efficient delivery process, with over 99% of orders completed within 60 minutes.

    • The average total delivery time is around 50 minutes (≈27 minutes for preparation and 23 minutes for delivery), showing good coordination between restaurant and logistics teams.

  • Customer Satisfaction and Ratings

    • Ratings are generally very positive, with most orders rated 4 or 5, and ~39% unrated.

    • Even delayed or long-duration orders still received high ratings, indicating that food quality and experience play a larger role than minor delivery delays.

  • Cuisine and Pricing Trends

    • American, Japanese, and Italian cuisines dominate the order volume (~70% of total orders).

    • French, Southern, and Thai cuisines have the highest average order cost (≈19 dollars), while Korean and Vietnamese are the most affordable.

    • Despite pricing differences, average ratings remain consistent across cuisines — customers seem equally satisfied regardless of cuisine type.

  • Weekday vs Weekend Performance

    • Weekend orders account for ~71% of all orders but have shorter delivery times (22.5 min) compared to weekdays (28.3 min).

    • Weekday operations show more delays, possibly due to traffic or work-hour congestion, but still maintain stable service levels.

  • Revenue and Commission Structure

    • The company generated 6,166.30 dollars in commission revenue.

    • 70% of orders fell in the 15% commission bracket, while 29% were in the 25% bracket, showing strong contribution from high-value orders.

  • Key Takeaways

    • Overall, the business shows excellent delivery consistency, strong customer satisfaction, and a healthy revenue model.

Recommendations:¶

  • Improve Weekday Delivery Efficiency

    • Focus on reducing weekday delivery times through better route optimization and driver allocation during peak lunch and evening hours.

    • Partner with logistics providers or use real-time traffic data to predict and avoid high-delay zones.

  • Encourage More Customer Ratings

    • With nearly 40% unrated orders, incentivize customers (e.g., through loyalty points or small discounts) to leave feedback. This would improve data quality for performance evaluation and help identify service gaps.

    • Introduce machine-learning-based sentiment analysis on textual feedback (if available) or post-delivery prompts for missing ratings.

  • Promote High-Rated and Popular Cuisines

    • Highlight American, Japanese, and Italian restaurants in marketing campaigns — they have high volume and strong ratings.

    • Also feature premium cuisines (French, Thai, Spanish) as “special experience” meals to attract higher-value customers.

  • Restaurant Performance Benchmarking

    • Identify top-rated restaurants (e.g., Shake Shack, Blue Ribbon Sushi Izakaya) and use them as benchmarks for service quality.

    • Use clustering analysis to segment restaurants into “High Performer,” “Improvement Needed,” and “Low Demand” categories.

    • Once we have Inmprovment Needed or Low Demand Restaurants provide trainings to standardize service quality or targeted personalized promotions.

  • Dynamic Commission or Incentive Model

    • Consider introducing tiered incentives — e.g., lower commission for restaurants maintaining high ratings and fast delivery times and driving volume.

    • Develop a predictive revenue model to simulate how changes in commission or pricing would affect total revenue.

    • This encourages restaurants to prioritize quality and speed, improving overall customer satisfaction.

  • Customer Segmentation & Marketing

    • Identity high-spend vs price-sensitive customers and push targeted personalized promotions where you can recommend diverse or premium cuisines to loyal high-spend customers. vs other reliable budget-friends options for other customers.

    • Develope association-rules example = “customers who ordered X often order Y” to show better suggestions for the customers.

  • Predictive Demand Forecasting

    • As we know, Weekends have 71% of total orders.

    • This information can be leveraged to optimize staffing, delivery capacity, and restaurant supply planning, ensuring smoother operations and better resource utilization during peak periods.
